pumac-2019-geometry-a-08.title: Poles, polars and two homotheties
pumac-2019-geometry-a-08.body:
**$PZ$ is tangent to $\Gamma$.** $P$ lies on $AB$, the polar of $C$, so $C$ lies on the polar of $P$ (La Hire). The polar of $P$ also passes through $X$ (as $PX$ is tangent), so it is line $CX$, which meets $\Gamma$ at the two tangency points from $P$: $X$ and $Z$. Hence $PZ$ is tangent and $PZ=PX=PY$.

**$Q$ is the midpoint of arc $AB$.** Since $PY=PZ$, there is a circle $\gamma'$ tangent to $PY$ at $Y$ and to $PZ$ at $Z$; it is internally tangent to $\Gamma$ at $Z$. The homothety at $Z$ taking $\gamma'$ to $\Gamma$ takes $Y$ to $Q$, and the tangent at $Q$ is parallel to $AB$, so $Q$ is the midpoint of arc $AB$: $QA=QB=6$.

**$XY$ bisects $\angle AXB$.** The same argument with the homothety at $X$ taking $\gamma$ to $\Gamma$ shows $XY$ passes through the midpoint of the arc $AB$ on the other side, so $\frac{AY}{YB}=\frac{AX}{XB}=\frac14$: $AY=2$, $YB=8$.

**Lengths.** By Stewart's theorem in the isosceles triangle $ABQ$, $QY^2=QA^2-AY\cdot YB=36-16=20$, so $QY=2\sqrt5$. Power of the point $Y$: $YZ=\frac{AY\cdot YB}{QY}=\frac{16}{2\sqrt5}=\frac{8}{\sqrt5}$. Therefore
$$QZ=2\sqrt5+\frac{8}{\sqrt5}=\frac{18}{\sqrt5}=\frac{18}{5}\sqrt5,$$
and $p+q+r=18+5+5=28$.

**Answer: 28**

pumac-2019-geometry-a-08.title: Shortcut once $Q$ is the arc midpoint
pumac-2019-geometry-a-08.body:
Once we know $Q$ is the midpoint of arc $AB$ (first approach), the triangles $QAY$ and $QZA$ are similar ($\angle QAB=\angle QBA=\angle QZA$, common angle at $Q$), so $QA^2=QY\cdot QZ$. Also $AY\cdot YB=16$ (whichever of $AY,YB$ is $2$) and Stewart's theorem gives $QY^2=QA^2-AY\cdot YB=20$. Hence
$$QZ=\frac{QA^2}{QY}=\frac{36}{2\sqrt5}=\frac{18\sqrt5}{5}.$$
(A numerical construction of a random configuration confirms $QA=QB$, $\frac{AX}{XB}=\frac{AY}{YB}$ and $QY^2=QA^2-AY\cdot YB$.)

**Answer: 28**
